# Atypicals and mycobacteria

> *A Gram stain of sputum from a student with pneumonia shows no predominant organism, a swab from a
> woman with no symptoms grows nothing on agar, and the culture from a man who has coughed for three
> months turns positive only after weeks. Each of these bacteria escapes the routine laboratory toolkit
> for a different reason, and the reason predicts how it is found and which drugs can reach it.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the atypical bacteria and the mycobacteria by why the routine toolkit fails on them, and
  predict from the reason how each is detected and which drugs can act on it.
- Explain why *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* causes a gradual pneumonia that spreads slowly through a
  household, and why drugs that act on the cell wall cannot treat it.
- Explain how *Chlamydia trachomatis* multiplies inside cells, and how a silent infection leads to
  infertility, ectopic pregnancy or blindness through scarring.
- Trace an infection with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* from inhaled bacteria to granuloma, latent
  infection and reactivation, and explain why active disease is treated with several drugs for months.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main organism cause disease.
- Tell *M. tuberculosis* from the non-tuberculous mycobacteria by source, spread and host.
:::

## The group {#sec-atyp-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-atyp-sentence}

The atypical bacteria and the mycobacteria are bacteria on which the routine Gram stain and culture on
agar fail, because they have no wall, grow only inside host cells, or have a waxy wall that resists the
Gram stain and grow slowly. Each reason also limits which drugs can reach them. In this course the
**atypical** bacteria are those grouped because routine stains and culture fail on them, either
because there is no cell wall or because the organism grows only inside host cells (see [*A map of
the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-atypicals)). The mycobacteria fail the same toolkit for a
third reason.

Three traits place a bacterium in the group:

- No cell wall: *Mycoplasma*, which shows nothing on a Gram stain and gives drugs that act on the wall
  no target
- Growth only inside host cells: *Chlamydia*, *Rickettsia* and *Orientia*, which are **obligate
  intracellular**, able to grow only inside living host cells, so they cannot be grown on agar
- A waxy wall: the mycobacteria, whose wall is packed with **mycolic acids**, the waxy wall component
  that resists the Gram stain, so they are detected with the **acid-fast stain**, a stain that detects
  organisms with waxy, mycolic-acid walls (see [*How bacteria are built and get
  energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope))

The mycobacteria of medical importance are *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Mycobacterium leprae* and
the **non-tuberculous mycobacteria**, mycobacteria other than those that cause tuberculosis and
leprosy, which live in water and soil. The members of the group are not closely related, so most of
the six questions have one answer for each of the three traits:

| Question | Answer for the atypicals and mycobacteria |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | *Mycoplasma*: a cell membrane stiffened with sterols, and no wall. *Chlamydia* and *Rickettsia*: an envelope of the Gram-negative type, with very little peptidoglycan in *Chlamydia*. Mycobacteria: a wall packed with mycolic acids |
| How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow? | *Mycoplasma* makes its own ATP and grows slowly on media enriched with sterols; *Chlamydia* and *Rickettsia* take ATP and nutrients from the host cell as well as making some ATP of their own; *M. tuberculosis* needs oxygen to make ATP |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; *Chlamydia* alternates between an infectious form outside cells and a dividing form inside them; *M. tuberculosis* divides about once a day and becomes resistant to drugs by mutation |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia trachomatis* and *M. tuberculosis* live only in humans and pass between people: in respiratory particles during close contact, by sexual contact and at birth, and through the air; *Rickettsia* and *Orientia* are carried by arthropods; non-tuberculous mycobacteria live in water and soil |
| How does damage happen? | Mostly through the host's response: inflammation of the airway and lung, scarring after repeated inflammation, and walled-off collections of macrophages with necrotic centres; *Rickettsia* and *Orientia* damage small blood vessels |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Bacterial ribosomes and enzymes, but no wall in *Mycoplasma*; drugs against the bacteria that live inside cells must first enter the host cell; mycobacteria have the enzymes that build mycolic acids, the target of one of the main drugs against tuberculosis |

### Sorting the group {#sec-atyp-key}

We sort the group first by why the routine toolkit fails, because that predicts how each member is
detected and which drugs can reach it, and then by where each member comes from, which predicts who
is exposed.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the atypicals and mycobacteria]{.tree-title}

- No cell wall: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*
- Growth only inside host cells
  - Passed by sexual contact, at birth or from eye to eye: *C. trachomatis*
  - Carried by ticks, lice or fleas: *Rickettsia*
  - Carried by mite larvae in rural scrub: *Orientia tsutsugamushi*
- A waxy, acid-fast wall: mycobacteria
  - From a person with active tuberculosis of the lungs: *M. tuberculosis*
  - From a person with untreated leprosy, after close and frequent contact: *M. leprae*
  - From water and soil: non-tuberculous mycobacteria
:::

Where stains and culture fail, most members are detected by a **nucleic acid amplification test
(NAAT)**, a test that copies a target sequence many times until it can be detected (see [*Detecting
and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-molecular)). The reason the
toolkit fails predicts the rest:

| Why the toolkit fails | Stain and culture | How it is usually detected | What follows for drugs |
|---|---|---|---|
| No cell wall | No Gram reaction; grows slowly on media enriched with sterols | NAAT | Drugs that act on the wall have nothing to act on |
| Growth only inside host cells | Not seen on a Gram stain; grows only in cultures of living cells | NAAT; for *Rickettsia* and *Orientia*, also the patient's antibodies (see [*Detecting and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)) | Drugs must cross the host cell's membrane to reach the bacteria |
| A waxy wall | Acid-fast; *M. tuberculosis* takes weeks to grow, and *M. leprae* cannot be grown in culture | Acid-fast stain, culture where it is possible, and NAAT | The wall keeps out many drugs, and slow growth means treatment lasts months |

Work through the key from why the routine toolkit fails, and read at each branch what the trait
predicts about the organism.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/atyp-key.yml"></div>

## Main organisms {#sec-atyp-main}

### *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*: a gradual pneumonia without a wall {#sec-atyp-mycoplasma}

*M. pneumoniae* has no cell wall, and its laboratory traits follow from that (see [*A map of the
bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-atypicals)). Mycoplasmas are the smallest free-living bacteria:
they make their own ATP and can grow without host cells, given sterols for their membrane.

*M. pneumoniae* lives only in humans and spreads in respiratory particles during close contact, in
families, schools and military barracks. Illness is commonest in school-age children, adolescents
and young adults. Its incubation period is long, often two to three weeks, so cases in a household
or a school appear one after another, weeks apart, as a propagated outbreak that can last for months
(see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-curves)). Immunity after an infection
does not last, so people can be infected again.

In the airway, *M. pneumoniae* attaches by a specialised tip to the ciliated cells lining the trachea
and bronchi and lies among their cilia. The hydrogen peroxide it releases damages the cells, the
cilia stop beating, and the damaged lining produces a dry cough that can last for weeks. In some
people the infection reaches the lungs. Lymphocytes gather around the small airways and in the walls
of the alveoli, while the air spaces stay largely free of pus. The pneumonia therefore comes on
gradually, and the patient often looks less ill than the chest X-ray suggests. Much of the damage
comes from the host's response (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).

The immune response can also act beyond the lung. Many patients make **cold agglutinins**, antibodies
that bind red blood cells below body temperature, and in a few these cause **haemolysis**, destruction
of red blood cells; some patients develop a rash or mouth ulcers.

::: {.example}
**Beta-lactams** are a family of drugs, named for the ring of atoms at their core, that block the
building of the peptidoglycan wall; the family includes the penicillins, the cephalosporins and the
carbapenems. They are a common first choice for pneumonia because the commonest bacterial causes have
a wall; in pneumonia caused by *M. pneumoniae* they have nothing to act on.
:::

*M. pneumoniae* harms the airway and lung in two ways:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Damage to the airway lining | The bacteria attach by their tip to ciliated cells; hydrogen peroxide damages the cells, and the cilia stop beating | A dry cough that lasts for weeks in a teenager |
| Pneumonia shaped by the host's response | Lymphocytes gather around the small airways and in the walls of the alveoli, and little pus fills the air spaces | A young adult who is still at work with a mild fever and a dry cough, whose chest X-ray shows more widespread changes than the examination suggested |

Three conditions let *M. pneumoniae* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | School-age children, adolescents and young adults; anyone can be infected again | Close contact exposes them, and immunity after an infection does not last |
| Where (setting) | Families, schools, university halls and military barracks | It lives only in humans and spreads in respiratory particles during close contact; a long incubation period stretches an outbreak over weeks to months |
| How (route) | Breathed in, to the ciliated cells of the trachea and bronchi, and in some people on to the lungs | It attaches by its tip and damages the cells; in the lungs, the host's inflammation causes the pneumonia |

Step through the route *M. pneumoniae* takes from one person's airway to the next.

### *Chlamydia trachomatis*: silent infection and scarring {#sec-atyp-chlamydia}

*C. trachomatis* is obligate intracellular and lives only in humans. Its envelope is of the
Gram-negative type with very little peptidoglycan, and it takes ATP and nutrients from the cell it
lives in (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-atypicals), where it is compared
with *M. pneumoniae*). It has two forms. The **elementary body** is a small, tough form that survives
outside cells and infects them but does not divide. The **reticulate body** is a larger form that divides inside a host cell but cannot survive
outside it. One cycle passes through both:

::: {.flow}
1. An elementary body attaches to an epithelial cell and is taken into it
2. Inside a membrane-bound vacuole, it turns into a reticulate body
3. Reticulate bodies take ATP and nutrients from the cell and divide by binary fission
4. Reticulate bodies turn back into elementary bodies
5. The cell bursts or releases the vacuole, and elementary bodies infect neighbouring cells or a new host
:::

Elementary bodies infect the epithelial cells of mucous membranes: in the cervix, the urethra and
the rectum, and in the conjunctiva, the membrane that covers the white of the eye and lines the
eyelids. *C. trachomatis* is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection worldwide. Most
infections in women, and many in men, cause no symptoms, so an infected person can carry the
bacterium for months and pass it to sexual partners without knowing.

In women, infection can cause **pelvic inflammatory disease**, infection and inflammation of the
uterus, fallopian tubes and nearby pelvic structures, usually spread up from the cervix. The bacterium kills the cells it infects as its elementary bodies are released,
but most of the lasting harm comes from the inflammation it provokes, which heals by scarring. Scarred, narrowed fallopian tubes can cause infertility, or an **ectopic
pregnancy**, a pregnancy that implants outside the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube. Immunity
after an infection is partial, so repeated infections are common, and each adds to the scarring.

::: {.example}
A woman who has never had symptoms of a genital infection can find, when she tries to conceive, that
both of her fallopian tubes are blocked by scarring from past infection.
:::

An infected mother can pass the bacterium to her infant during a vaginal birth. The **neonate**, a
newborn infant in the first four weeks of life, can develop **conjunctivitis**, inflammation of the
conjunctiva, in the first weeks after birth, and some infants develop pneumonia in the first months.

Other strains of *C. trachomatis* infect the eye and pass from child to child on hands, cloths and
flies, where water for washing is scarce. These eye infections recur throughout childhood, and the
result is **trachoma**, chronic inflammation of the conjunctiva from repeated infection of the eye
with *C. trachomatis*, which in time scars the eyelids and cornea. The scarred inner surface of the
eyelids contracts, the eyelashes turn inwards and scratch the cornea, and the scarred cornea becomes
opaque. Trachoma is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, and it persists in poor rural
communities, most of them in Africa.

A third set of strains causes **lymphogranuloma venereum**, a sexually transmitted infection in which
*C. trachomatis* invades beyond the epithelium and spreads in lymph to the regional lymph nodes. The
lymph nodes of the groin swell and become painful or, after anal sex, the rectum becomes inflamed.

Because most infections are silent, testing people without symptoms by NAAT on urine or a genital
swab, and treating their sexual partners, finds and stops infections that would otherwise spread.

*C. trachomatis* does most of its harm in four ways, and its lasting damage is scarring:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Infection of the cervix or urethra | Elementary bodies infect the epithelium and multiply in its cells; the inflammation is often too mild to notice | Discomfort on passing urine and a discharge in a man, or no symptoms at all, especially in a woman, who passes the infection to partners unknowingly |
| Scarring of the fallopian tubes | Infection spreads up to the fallopian tubes; persistent or repeated inflammation heals by scarring, which narrows or blocks them | Infertility, or an ectopic pregnancy, in a woman who never had symptoms |
| Infection of the neonate | Elementary bodies in the mother's cervix reach the infant's conjunctiva and nasopharynx during a vaginal birth | Conjunctivitis with a discharge in the first weeks after birth |
| Trachoma | Repeated infection of the conjunctiva scars the eyelids, which turn the lashes inwards against the cornea | Blindness in an adult who had repeated eye infections as a child, in a community short of water |

Three conditions let *C. trachomatis* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A sexually active adult, especially a young adult; a neonate born to an infected mother; for trachoma, a child in a community short of water | Most infections are silent, so they pass undetected between partners and to infants at birth; immunity is partial, so infection recurs |
| Where (setting) | Sexual contact with a partner who has no symptoms; a vaginal birth; for trachoma, households where faces are seldom washed and flies gather | It lives only in humans and passes in genital or eye secretions |
| How (route) | Elementary bodies reach a mucous membrane and enter its epithelial cells | It multiplies inside the cells and spreads up the genital tract; repeated inflammation heals by scarring |

Step through the two routes of *C. trachomatis*: a silent sexual infection, and infection of a
neonate during birth.

### *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*: containment, latency and reactivation {#sec-atyp-tuberculosis}

*M. tuberculosis* has a waxy, mycolic-acid wall, needs oxygen and divides only about once a day (see
[*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-growth)). Humans are its
reservoir. A person with active tuberculosis of the lungs coughs out bacteria in particles small
enough to stay suspended in the air of a room, so it spreads by **airborne transmission**, spread by
small exhaled particles that stay suspended in air and can travel beyond a metre or two (see
[*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)). A few inhaled bacteria can
start an infection, so the risk depends on how long a person shares the air of an enclosed space with
an infectious person, and on how well the space is ventilated. Tuberculosis remains common in
Singapore and throughout South-East Asia.

*M. tuberculosis* is **facultative intracellular**, able to live both inside and outside host cells,
and in the body it lives mainly inside macrophages. Macrophages in the alveoli engulf the inhaled
bacteria, but the bacteria stop the vacuole that holds them from fusing with lysosomes, and they
survive and multiply inside (see [*How bacteria cause
damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-evade)). Before an
immune response develops, infected macrophages carry some bacteria in lymph to the lymph nodes at the
root of the lung, and some bacteria reach other organs in the blood.

Control depends on **cell-mediated immunity**, the defence by T cells against infected cells and
against organisms that live inside host cells. Over the following weeks, T cells that recognise the
bacterium activate the macrophages, which gather around the infected cells to form a **granuloma**, a
compact collection of activated macrophages, surrounded by lymphocytes, that walls off an organism the
macrophages cannot kill (see [*How bacteria cause damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-host)). The
centre of a granuloma often undergoes **caseous necrosis**, necrosis that leaves a soft, cheese-like
mass of dead cells.

In most people the granulomas contain the infection. A few bacteria survive within them for years or
decades without causing symptoms: a **latent infection**, persistence of an organism in a silent
state, with the possibility of reactivation (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)). A person with latent infection has no
bacteria in the airways and does not infect others.

::: {.flow}
1. Inhaled bacteria reach the alveoli
2. Macrophages engulf them, and the bacteria survive and multiply inside
3. T cells activate the macrophages, which wall the bacteria into granulomas
4. A few bacteria survive, silent, inside the granulomas: latent infection
5. If cell-mediated immunity fails, the bacteria multiply again and destroy lung tissue: active tuberculosis
:::

The lifetime risk that latent infection becomes active disease is about 5–10%, and it rises when
cell-mediated immunity fails (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)):

- HIV infection, which destroys the T cells that direct the response, so the risk rises from early in
  the infection and climbs as the T cells are lost (described later, in [*Viruses and the
  host*](../viruses/virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cd4))
- Diabetes
- Older age
- Drugs that suppress immunity, such as those given after an organ transplant

Young children, whose cell-mediated immunity is immature, more often progress from infection
straight to disease. In them the bacteria can spread through the body in the blood and reach the
meninges, causing tuberculous **meningitis**, inflammation of the meninges, the membranes that cover
the brain and spinal cord.

In active tuberculosis of the lungs, usually in their upper parts, the bacteria multiply in the
granulomas and the caseous centres enlarge. When a centre liquefies and drains into a bronchus, it
leaves a cavity in the lung whose wall holds very large numbers of bacteria, and coughing carries them
into the air. The illness develops over weeks to months, with a cough, fever, night sweats and weight
loss. Damage comes from both the bacterium and the host's response (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)): when the response is weak the bacteria
spread, and when it is strong it destroys lung tissue.

Three methods find *M. tuberculosis* in sputum, and a trait of the bacterium limits each one:

- The acid-fast stain gives a result within hours but needs many bacteria in the sample (see
  [*Detecting bacteria and testing susceptibility*](detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-microscopy))
- Culture takes weeks, because the bacterium divides slowly, but yields an isolate that can be tested
  against drugs (see [*Detecting bacteria and testing
  susceptibility*](detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-culture))
- A NAAT detects its DNA, and some of the mutations that make it resistant to drugs, within hours

Latent infection leaves no bacteria to find in sputum, so it is detected by tests of the T-cell
response to the bacterium, given as a skin test or a blood test. A positive result means that a
person has probably been infected, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease. A skin
test can also turn positive after exposure to non-tuberculous mycobacteria, and both tests can be
falsely negative when cell-mediated immunity is weak.

Active tuberculosis is treated for several months with **combination therapy**, treatment with two or
more drugs acting on different targets, so that a variant resistant to one is still suppressed by the
others. Two traits of the bacterium explain this:

- A cavity holds so many bacteria that some already carry a mutation that makes them resistant to any
  one drug, and a single drug would select them; in *M. tuberculosis* resistance arises by mutation,
  without gene transfer (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
  change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mutation))
- Bacteria that divide slowly, or barely at all, inside granulomas and necrotic tissue are killed
  slowly, so treatment must continue for months

Treatment that is stopped early or taken irregularly selects resistant bacteria, and resistant
strains then spread to other people. Strains resistant to several of the main drugs are much harder
to treat.

Three measures prevent tuberculosis:

- Finding and treating people with active tuberculosis of the lungs, which stops the spread
- Tracing and testing their contacts, and treating latent infection to prevent reactivation
- Vaccinating infants

The **BCG vaccine** (bacille Calmette–Guérin), a live vaccine made from a weakened strain of a
mycobacterium closely related to *M. tuberculosis*, is given at birth in Singapore (see [*Detecting
and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)). It protects young
children against the severe forms of tuberculosis, in which the bacteria spread through the body or
reach the meninges, but it protects less reliably against tuberculosis of the lungs in adults, the
form that spreads the infection. Because BCG is itself a mycobacterium, it can also turn the skin test
positive; blood tests that use bacterial proteins absent from BCG avoid this.

*M. tuberculosis* does its harm in three ways, set by how well cell-mediated immunity contains it:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Latent infection | T cells and activated macrophages wall the bacteria into granulomas, where a few survive, multiplying little or not at all | No symptoms; a positive test of the T-cell response in a healthy adult whose household member has active tuberculosis |
| Active tuberculosis of the lungs | When cell-mediated immunity fails, the bacteria multiply again; caseous centres liquefy and drain into a bronchus, leaving cavities full of bacteria | A cough for two months, with fever, night sweats and weight loss, and a cavity in the upper part of a lung |
| Spread beyond the lungs | Bacteria carried in lymph and blood settle in lymph nodes, the meninges, bones and other organs, especially when cell-mediated immunity is immature or fails | Tuberculous meningitis in a young child; enlarged lymph nodes in the neck of an adult |

Three conditions let *M. tuberculosis* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone who inhales it can be infected; active disease is most likely when cell-mediated immunity is immature or fails: young children, people with HIV infection or diabetes, older adults, people taking drugs that suppress immunity | T cells that activate macrophages contain the bacteria in granulomas; when they are lacking, the bacteria multiply |
| Where (setting) | Prolonged sharing of air with a person who has active tuberculosis of the lungs, in a household or a crowded, poorly ventilated space | Infectious particles stay suspended in still air; people with latent infection do not spread it |
| How (route) | Inhaled into the alveoli and engulfed by macrophages | It survives inside macrophages, travels in lymph and blood before immunity develops, and can stay latent for decades |

::: {.callout-important}
## Can a person with latent tuberculosis infection pass it on?
The word "tuberculosis" is used for both the infection and the disease, so a positive test for
tuberculosis is often taken to mean that a person is infectious, and people with latent infection can
meet the same caution as those with active disease. In latent infection the bacteria are held in
granulomas in the lung, none reach the airway, and nothing is coughed out, so the person does not
infect others. Only active disease of the lungs or airway puts the bacteria into the air.
:::

Step through the two routes of *M. tuberculosis*: containment and reactivation in an adult, and
spread through the body in a young child.

## Contrast pair {#sec-atyp-pairs}

### *M. tuberculosis* and non-tuberculous mycobacteria {#sec-atyp-pair-tb-ntm}

*M. tuberculosis* and the non-tuberculous mycobacteria share the waxy wall and look alike on an
acid-fast stain of sputum, so the laboratory tells them apart by identifying the species, in culture
or by NAAT. Compare them feature by feature before reading the principle.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-tb-ntm.yml"></div>

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-atyp-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-atyp-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Rickettsia* | Ticks, lice and fleas (and, for a few species, mites), and the animals or people they feed on; reaches humans through the arthropod's bite, or its faeces rubbed into the skin | Obligate intracellular; grows free in the cytoplasm of the cells lining small blood vessels | Causes fever, headache and often a rash, as infected small blood vessels become inflamed and leak; a tick bite can leave a dark scab; drugs must enter host cells to reach it |
| *Orientia tsutsugamushi* | Larval mites in scrub and grassland in rural Asia and the western Pacific, including South-East Asia; the mites pass it to their eggs, so they maintain it in nature as well as carrying it to people | Obligate intracellular; once classified as a species of *Rickettsia* | Causes **scrub typhus**, a fever with headache after the bite of an infected mite larva, often with an **eschar**, a dark scab at the site of the painless bite; a common cause of fever in rural parts of the region, which can be severe or fatal without treatment |
| *M. leprae* | Humans; passed during close and frequent contact with a person with untreated leprosy, probably in respiratory particles from the nose and mouth | Cannot be grown in culture; grows best below body temperature, in the skin and peripheral nerves of the cooler parts of the body; divides far more slowly than *M. tuberculosis*, so disease appears years after infection | Causes **leprosy**, chronic infection of the skin and peripheral nerves by *M. leprae*. Damage to the nerves causes loss of sensation, and unnoticed injuries lead to deformity. A strong cell-mediated response gives a few skin patches with few bacteria, a weak one widespread lesions full of bacteria |
| Non-tuberculous mycobacteria | Water and soil, including the biofilms inside water pipes and showerheads | Acid-fast, like *M. tuberculosis*; not usually passed between people; naturally resistant to many drugs | Chronic lung infection in damaged lungs; skin and wound infections after injections, surgery or tattoos; infection that spreads through the body in advanced HIV infection |

### Later in the course {#sec-atyp-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* | Respiratory medicine and paediatrics (pneumonia in children and young adults); pharmacology (drugs for pneumonia caused by bacteria without a wall) |
| *C. trachomatis* | Sexual health; obstetrics and gynaecology (pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility and ectopic pregnancy); neonatology and ophthalmology (conjunctivitis in the neonate; trachoma) |
| *M. tuberculosis* | Respiratory medicine (tuberculosis of the lungs); neurology (tuberculous meningitis); public health (contact tracing and treatment of latent infection); HIV care; pharmacology (combination treatment and resistance) |
| *Rickettsia* and *O. tsutsugamushi* | Infectious diseases and travel medicine (fever with a rash or an eschar) |
| *M. leprae* | Dermatology and neurology (skin patches with loss of sensation; damage to peripheral nerves) |
| Non-tuberculous mycobacteria | Respiratory medicine (lung infection in damaged lungs); dermatology (skin infection after procedures); HIV care |
